deed: סידני ברנר וביסוס הצ׳-אלגנס כאורגניזם מודל
title: Sydney Brenner and turning the C. elegans worm into a model organism

trailer.text: According to Hamichlol, Sydney Brenner was a Jewish South African biologist, and one of the three laureates of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Brenner said that he was interested in the nervous system and wanted to find a simple experimental system that would show how brains are constructed.
According to Nature and Britannica, he chose the nematode worm C. elegans, which is simple enough to study in depth, transparent, reproduces quickly and is inexpensive to maintain.
According to Nature, turning the worm into a model system for human-disease research in the 1960s and 1970s opened a new field of research.
In 2002 Brenner shared the Nobel Prize with Robert Horvitz and John Sulston, who, according to the Simons Foundation, were postdoctoral fellows in his lab.

paragraphs.text: According to South African History Online, Sydney Brenner was born on 13 January 1927 in Germiston, close to Johannesburg, to Jewish parents.
Brenner said that his father came to South Africa from Lithuania in 1910, and his mother came from Latvia in 1922.
According to Hamichlol, his father emigrated to avoid conscription into the Tsar's army.
Brenner said that his father was a shoemaker, and that their first home was in rooms at the back of the shop.
Brenner said that the Germiston Town Council gave him a bursary of 60 pounds per year, which allowed him to study medicine at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg.
According to him, in his final year of studies he failed Medicine, barely passed Surgery, and received a First Class in Obstetrics and Gynecology.

stations.title: Oxford, Cambridge and the genetic code

paragraphs.text: Brenner said that at Oxford he and his friends were outsiders three times over: scientists, research students and colonials.
According to him, the moment he saw the DNA model and heard about base pairing, he realized that it was the key to problems in biology that had seemed intractable.
Brenner said that Francis Crick worked to get him an appointment at the Medical Research Council Unit in Cambridge, and in December 1956 he left for England.
He said that he shared an office with Crick for 20 years, and that many ideas, right and wrong, were generated from their conversations.
Crick wrote that Brenner was better than he was at thinking up novel experiments, and that he himself served mainly as a critic and clarifier.
According to the Simons Foundation, Brenner's most famous experiment was carried out in 1960 with François Jacob in Meselson's laboratory at Caltech, and demonstrated the existence of mRNA.
According to Hamichlol, the discovery of mRNA earned Brenner the 1971 Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research.
According to Asian Scientist, in 1961 Brenner, Crick and others used a bacteriophage system to show that the genetic code is composed of non-overlapping triplets.
According to Nature, these triplets of nucleotides are called codons.
According to Nature, in 1964 Brenner was a founding member of EMBO.

stations.title: Looking for a simple animal to understand a brain

paragraphs.text: Brenner said that he was interested in the nervous system and wanted to find a simple experimental system that would show how brains are constructed.
According to the Simons Foundation, he wrote to Perutz that he wanted to "tame" a small metazoan organism, to study development directly.
According to Nature, he chose the nematode worm C. elegans because it is more complex than well-understood organisms such as bacteria, yet simple enough to study in depth.
According to the Leopoldina, in 1963 Brenner described the worm, in an application, as a good organism for his research.
According to the Leopoldina, the worm is one millimetre long, it is transparent, and it lives about 20 days.
According to Britannica, the transparency makes it possible to follow cell divisions under a microscope, and the worm reproduces quickly and is inexpensive to maintain.
According to the Simons Foundation, in 1974, ten years after beginning work on the worm, Brenner published a paper describing some 300 mutants.
According to the Foundation, this was his most influential paper, with more than 6,000 citations.
According to the Simons Foundation, Brenner's lab mapped the wiring of the worm's nervous system using electron microscopy, and the work led to a 340-page monograph in 1986.

stations.title: 959 cells, a Nobel Prize and a new field

paragraphs.text: According to the Simons Foundation, John Sulston and Robert Horvitz, postdoctoral fellows in the lab, traced the lineage of all 959 cells of the adult worm and the lineage of the embryo cells.
According to Britannica, programmed cell death eliminates 131 cells in the worm, so that 959 body cells remain in the adult.
According to Asian Scientist, the researchers identified genes that control programmed cell death in worms, and opened a way to studying its regulation in humans.
According to the Leopoldina, understanding cell death is important for medicine, because apoptotic processes are involved in many diseases, including heart disease and degenerative diseases.
The 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded jointly to Brenner, Horvitz and Sulston.
According to Hamichlol, that same year, shortly before the Nobel Prize, Brenner won the Dan David Prize from Tel Aviv University.
According to the Leopoldina, in 1987 Brenner received the Harvey Prize of the Technion - Israel Institute of Technology.
According to Nature, turning the worm into a model system for human-disease research opened a new field of research.
According to Nature, the PubMed database lists some 15,000 papers from the past decade that mention the worm.

stations.title: Singapore, the fugu and a new institute

paragraphs.text: According to Asian Scientist, on a visit to Singapore in 1984 Brenner told Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew that if they did not establish such a research institution, they would remain a nation of technicians.
According to the Simons Foundation, with his encouragement the Singapore government focused on basic biological research, opened an institute in 1987 and completed Biopolis in 2003.
According to Hamichlol, he guided the Singapore government in the early stages of its biomedical research.
According to Asian Scientist, in 2003 Brenner was made an honorary citizen of Singapore, for his contribution to putting the country on the world map of biomedical research.
According to Genome Research, the fugu genome was sequenced and published in 2002 by an international consortium that Brenner assembled and led.
According to Asian Scientist, Brenner called it the "discount genome," because it offered a 90 percent discount on the cost of sequencing.
According to Asian Scientist, Brenner developed with Sam Eletr a technique for parallel sequencing of DNA molecules on microscopic beads.
Brenner said that he founded the Molecular Sciences Institute with a gift from the Philip Morris Company.
According to Britannica, the institute is in California.

stations.title: The man and the people he raised

paragraphs.text: Brenner wrote that a scientist should be judged by the quality of the people he helped to produce, and not by prizes or honours.
According to Hamichlol, a related nematode is now named after him: Caenorhabditis brenneri.
According to Asian Scientist, Brenner was married to May until her death in 2010.
According to Asian Scientist, Brenner died in Singapore on 5 April 2019, at the age of 92.
According to the Simons Foundation, Brenner considers his appointment as director of the laboratory in 1979 one of the biggest mistakes of his life.
According to the Simons Foundation, opponents of the approach of sequencing coding regions argued that it would miss noncoding regions that control gene expression.
According to Genome Research, Brenner replied with humour that he had changed his mind, and that he now thinks 98% of the human genome is "junk."

Asian Scientist: 58 years, until May's death in 2010

claims.text: לפי Genome Research, ברנר ענה בהומור שהוא שינה את דעתו ועכשיו הוא חושב ש-98% מהגנום האנושי הם 'זבל'.
claims.quote: No, I have changed my mind. Now I think that only 98% of the human genome is junk.

claims.text: לפי המכלול, ברנר היה הראשון שהשתמש ב-1965 בתולעת הנימית הקטנה והשקופה למחקר.
claims.quote: ברנר היה הראשון שהשתמש, ב-1965, בתולעת נימית עגולה, שקופה וקטנה

claims.text: לפי המכלול, נישואיו של ברנר נמשכו 57 שנים עד מות אשתו בינואר 2010.
claims.quote: נישואין אלה נמשכו חמישים ושבע שנים, עד פטירתה של אשתו בינואר 2010
